FINDINGS OF FACT 
These proposed revisions to the findings of fact and conclusions of law are focused on those aspects of the proposed order that address the alternative PFD recommendation of route selection.

Description of the Proposed Routes
Applicants filed 122 alternative routes for the Commission’s consideration.
The proposed transmission line is approximately 214 to 244 miles in length depending on the route.
Applicants identified Route 894, and Commission Staff identified Route 487, as the route that best addresses the applicable routing factors of PURA and the Commission’s rules.
Should a route be selected for construction, the Route .
Routing Criteria
The project team of Halff and Kimley-Horn, Applicants’ environmental consultants, included professionals with expertise in different environmental and land use disciplines who were involved in data acquisition, routing analysis, and environmental assessment of the transmission facilities.
To identify preliminary alternative route links for the proposed transmission line, Halff and Kimley-Horn delineated a study area, sought public official and agency input, gathered data regarding the study area, and performed constraints mapping.
Route  894comprised of route links






A0, A1, A2, B1, B21, C4, D12, C5, E52, F1, F31, F32, F20, F23, G72, G73, G82, G13, G51, G52, H1, H41, H42, J21,J22, J23, J27, J4, K11, K7, J16, K13, K51, K52, M11, M12, N3, P2, R1, T1, T2, and Z2

Route presents an appropriate balance of routing factors, and any negative attributes can be addressed with mitigation and the application of best-practice engineering design and construction methods.
Estimated Costs
The estimated construction costs for the 122 filed routes range from approximately $1,636,232,000 to $1,857,768,000, excluding station costs.
Regardless of the selected route, the estimated cost of the station work proposed in the Application for construction of a new 765-kV switchyard at Bell County East Switch is $395,468,000.
The estimated cost for Route is , excluding station costs.
The total estimated cost to construct the proposed Project, including station costs, along Route  is .
Should a route be selected for construction, Oncor intends to finance the proposed Project through a combination of debt and equity. LCRA’s portion of the proposed Project may be financed through a combination of tax-exempt commercial paper, tax-exempt private revolving note, or taxable commercial paper, and subsequent to project completion, fixed-rate debt.
Prudent Avoidance
Rule 25.101(a)(6) defines prudent avoidance as the “limiting of exposures to electric and magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort.”
Route  has  known habitable structures located within 500 feet of its centerline.
Route  complies with the Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance.

Community Values
Information regarding community values was received from local, state, and federal agencies and incorporated into the routing analysis and the transmission line’s route selection.
Applicants held three public participation meetings, which resulted in the submission of completed questionnaires or other correspondence indicating primary concerns relating to community values.
A total of 825 members of the public signed in as attendees at the public participation meetings, and 189 attendees filled out questionnaires at the public meetings, and numerous questionnaires and other correspondence were received following the meetings via mail, email, or phone.
Following the public participation meetings and associated correspondence and investigations, Kimley-Horn and Halff made preliminary route link additions, removals, and modifications. Such modifications led to an expansion of the breadth of alternative route links to include alternatives further north in Lampasas, San Saba, and McCulloch counties, Texas.
A summary of comments from federal, state, and local officials and agencies is provided in the EA.
Applicants assessed preliminary route links and possible modifications after evaluating community feedback.
Among other things, community values in the study area expressed concern about effects to residences, ranching, aesthetics, property values, the environment, the use/presence of existing transmission lines, health concerns, fish and wildlife, historic resources, flood protection, and development.

Route  addresses the expressed community values.

Use of Existing Corridors / Paralleling
The 122 alternative routes filed with the Application use or parallel existing compatible ROW and apparent property boundaries for a range of approximately 32.1% to 54.1% of the route lengths.
Applicants evaluated the use and paralleling of existing compatible ROW and apparent property boundaries when developing alternative routes filed with the Application.




Route  uses or parallels existing compatible ROW to a reasonable extent in consideration of the total balancing of routing factors.
Engineering Constraints

Applicants evaluated engineering and construction constraints when developing their alternative routes.
Applicants’ evaluation of engineering-related constraints is limited to the knowledge that can be obtained using resources available prior to project approval. Once approved, Applicants may identify additional constraints through boring and surveying that inform final design and construction activities such as specific structure siting.
Applicants did not identify any engineering constraints that would prevent the construction of transmission facilities along Route .
Land Uses and Land Types
Radio Towers and Other Electronic Installations
There are no commercial AM radio transmitters located within 10,000 feet of Route .
There are FM radio transmitters, microwave, and other electronic installations located within 2,000 feet of the centerline of Route .Should a route be selected for construction, it is unlikely that the presence of transmission facilities along Route  will adversely affect communication operations in the proximity of the route.
Airstrips and Airports
There are three airports registered with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) with a runway 3,200 feet or shorter in length and within 10,000 feet of the centerline of Route .
There are airports registered with the FAA with at least one runway longer than 3,200 feet in length and within 20,000 feet of Route ’s centerline.
There are  known private airstrips located within 10,000 feet of the centerline of Route .
There are  heliports located within 5,000 feet of the centerline of Route 
Irrigation Systems
Route  crosses agricultural croplands with known mobile irrigation systems for  miles.
Should a route be selected for construction, it is unlikely that the presence of transmission facilities along Route  will adversely affect any agricultural lands with known mobile irrigation systems.
Recreational and Park Areas
Route  does not cross any parks or recreational areas.
There are no known parks or recreational areas located within 1,000 feet of Route ’s centerline.

Aesthetic Values
An estimated miles of Route ’s ROW is located within the foreground visual zone of U.S. or state highways.
Route  minimizes impacts to aesthetic values to a reasonable extent while balancing the Commission’s routing criteria.
Historical and Archaeological Values
Route  crosses recorded cultural historical sites.
There are  recorded cultural sites located with 1,000 feet of Route s centerline.
Route  crosses areas with high potential for historical or archeological sites for  miles, or  of its length.
Route  minimizes impacts to historical and archeological resources to a reasonable extent while balancing the Commission’s routing criteria.
Environmental Integrity
The EA analyzed the possible effects of the transmission facilities on numerous environmental factors.
Kimley-Horn and Halff evaluated the effects of the transmission facilities on the environment.
Kimley-Horn and Halff evaluated potential consequences for soil and water resources, the ecosystem (including endangered and threatened vegetation and fish and wildlife), and land use within the study area.
Should a route be selected for construction, it is unlikely that constructing the proposed Project will significantly affect soil resources, water resources, wetland resources, ecological resources, endangered and threatened species, or land use.
Route  crosses  miles of cropland/hay meadow and miles of rangeland/pasture.
No part of Route  crosses upland woodlands.
Route  crosses riparian areas for miles.
Route crosses potential wetlands for  miles.
There are  stream crossings on Route .
Route  is parallel to streams.
Route crosses open water for  miles.
Route  crosses known habitat of federally listed endangered or threatened species for  miles.
Should a route be selected for construction, Applicants will mitigate any effect on federally or state-listed plant or animal species according to standard practices and measures taken in accordance with the Endangered Species Act.
Should a route be selected for construction, it is appropriate for Applicants to minimize the amount of flora and fauna disturbed during construction of the transmission facilities.
Should a route be selected for construction, it is appropriate for Applicants to re-vegetate cleared and disturbed areas using native species and to consider landowner preferences and wildlife needs in doing so.
Should a route be selected for construction, it is appropriate for Applicants to avoid, to the maximum extent reasonably possible, causing adverse environmental effects on sensitive plant and animal species and their habitats as identified by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and TPWD.
Should a route be selected for construction, it is appropriate for Applicants to implement erosion control measures and return each affected landowner’s property to its original contours and grades unless the landowners agree otherwise. However, it is not appropriate for Applicants to restore original contours and grades where different contours and grades are necessary to ensure the safety or stability of any transmission line’s structures or the safe operation and maintenance of any transmission line.
Should a route be selected for construction, it is appropriate for Applicants to exercise extreme care to avoid affecting non-targeted vegetation or animal life when using chemical herbicides to control vegetation within rights-of-way. The use of chemical herbicides to control vegetation within rights-of-way is required to comply with the rules and guidelines established in the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act and with the Texas Department of Agriculture’s regulations.
Should a route be selected for construction, it is appropriate for Applicants to protect raptors and migratory birds by following the procedures outlined in the following publications: Reducing Avian Collisions with Power Lines: State of the Art in 2012, Edison Electric Institute and Avian Power Line Interaction Committee, Washington, D.C. 2012; Suggested Practices for Avian Protection on Power Lines: The State of the Art in 2006, Edison Electric Institute, Avian Power Line Interaction Committee, and California Energy Commission, Washington, D.C. and Sacramento, CA 2006; and the Avian Protection Plan Guidelines, Avian Power Line Interaction Committee and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, April 2005. It is appropriate for Applicants to take precautions to avoid disturbing occupied nests and take steps to minimize the burden of construction on migratory birds during the nesting season of the migratory bird species identified in the area of construction.
Should a route be selected for construction, it is appropriate for Applicants to use best management practices to minimize any potential harm that Route  presents to migratory birds and threatened or endangered species.
Should a route be selected for construction, it is unlikely that the presence of transmission facilities along Route  will have a significant adverse effect on the environmental integrity of the surrounding landscape.
Route presents an appropriate balance between environmental integrity and the routing considerations identified in PURA and the Commission’s rules.

XIII. 	CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
Oncor is a public utility as defined in PURA § 11.004 and an electric utility as defined in PURA § 31.002(6).
LCRA is a public utility as defined in PURA § 11.004 and an electric utility as defined in PURA § 31.002(6).
The Commission has authority over this matter under PURA §§ 14.001, 32.001, 37.051, .053, .054, and .056.
Applicants are required to obtain the Commission’s approval to construct the proposed transmission facilities and provide service to the public using those facilities. PURA § 37.053.
Bell County East Switch and Big Hill Substation are existing electric utility facilities under PURA § 37.056(e).
SOAH exercised jurisdiction over the proceeding under PURA § 14.053 and Texas Government Code §§ 2003.021 and 2003.049.
The Application is sufficient under Rule 22.75(d).
Applicants provided notice of the Application in compliance with Rule 22.52(a)(1).
Applicants complied with the requirements of Rule 22.52(a)(2).
Applicants did not comply with the notice requirements of Rule 22.52(a)(3).
Applicants did not comply with the requirements of Rule 22.52(a)(4).
The hearing on the merits was set, and notice of the hearing was provided, in compliance with PURA § 37.054 and Texas Government Code §§ 2001.051 and 2001.052
ERCOT’s PBRP recommendation is not entitled to great weight in the determination of need for this reliability project. 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II).
The evidence does not establish that amendment of Applicants’ respective CCNs is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public. PURA § 37.056. As a result, Applications for Bell County East-to-Big Hill and Big Hill-to-Sand Lake Projects should be denied.
The evidence establishes the Application should be denied for Applicants’ failure to comply with the process due to approximately 1,400 landowners under Rule 22.52(a)(4) for public meeting, to their prejudice.
Should a route be selected for construction, Route  provides the best balance of the routing consideration factors of PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B), including the Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance, to the extent reasonable to moderate the impact on the affected community and landowners.
17.	The Application provided an adequate number of reasonably differentiated alternative routes for the Commission to conduct a proper evaluation.
PROPOSED ORDERING PARAGRAPHS
The Commission adopts the proposal for decision, including findings of fact and conclusions of law, to the extent provided in this Order.
The Commission does not approve the Applications for the Bell County East-to-Big Hill and Big Hill-to-Sand Lake Projects. The amendment of Applicants’ CCNs is not approved by this Order.
The Commission denies all other motions and any other requests for general or specific relief that the Commission has not expressly granted.
